title.value: A New Model for the Simulation of Naturally Fractured Reservoirs

name.value: Stanford University, Department of Petroleum Engineering

note.value: Naturally fractured reservoirs are normally idealized by a set of disconnected matrix blocks within a network of connected fractures. The matrix system stores most of the fluids and feeds the fractures that are responsible for transport throughout the reservoir. These characteristics have led to the double porosity approach used in many simulators. This double porosity approach considers only matrix-fracture and fracture-fracture flow, unlike the double permeability approach that also allows matrix-matrix flow. In numerical models, computational work is usually minimized by eliminating matrix unknowns from the fracture equations before they are solved by direct or iterative methods. Most such models, however, are incapable of simulating the transient nature of imbibition. In this work a new model is presented for the simulation of naturally fractured reservoirs. The model neither increases the number of equations per block nor requires Gaussian elimination to decouple matrix unknowns from fracture unknowns. This is attained by a single analytically derived transfer function that depends only on the fracture variables, and by the assumption of instantaneous pressure equilibrium. The new analytical transfer function was derived considering capillary pressure as the only driving force of the process, and eliminating the matrix saturation from the fracture flow equations. The assumption of instantaneous pressure equilibrium eliminates the matrix pressure. The resulting model, therefore, has the same form as standard single porosity models. The results of the new model are compared with those from published laboratory experiments, fine grid simulations of matrix-fracture transfer or a single matrix block, and simulation of field-scale problems by standard double porosity models. The new model showed good agreement with the Kleppe and Morse's (1974) high rate experiment, and a perfect match for the low rate case. The model was used also to duplicate fine grid simulations of single matrix blocks surrounded by both water and gas. The same good results were obtained, and in the oil/water cases the match was better for high capillary pressure curves. Gravity affects the transient of both drainage and imbibition processes according to the block height. It was observed that gravity decreases the transient period for the smallest blocks and increases it for the largest blocks. Simulation of field-scale examples includes water flooding a five-spot pattern, a line drive and a cross-section. The case of depleting a reservoir using a two-dimensional cross-section gridding was also simulated. The results using the new model were close to those from other models presented in the literature. These results demonstrate that the new model provides an economical and accurate means of predicting performance of fractured reservoirs in both oil/water and gas/oil systems.
Dutra, Jr., Tarcilio Viana. (1991). A New Model for the Simulation of Naturally Fractured Reservoirs. Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: http://purl.stanford.edu/dj364mf9718
